en: The Path of Discrimination 3:
The Chapter on Wisdom 3.8.
Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness.
Which four?"

"Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. [He dwells] contemplating feelings...
the mind..."
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
These, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness.
How does one dwell contemplating the body in the body?
Here, someone contemplates the body of earth as impermanent, not as permanent;
he contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasure;
he contemplates it as non-self, not as self.
One becomes disenchanted, not delighted;
one becomes dispassionate, not passionate;
one brings to cessation, not to origination; one relinquishes, not grasps.
Contemplating impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure;
contemplating non-self, one abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust;
bringing about cessation, one abandons origination; relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
One contemplates the body in these seven aspects.
The body is the foundation, but not the mindfulness;
mindfulness is both the foundation and the mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that body.
Therefore, it is called "the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body."
"Bhāvanā" means four kinds of development:

there is development in the sense of non-transgression of the states arisen therein; development in the sense of the single function of the faculties; development in the sense of the exertion of energy directed toward that; and development in the sense of repetition.
Herein, someone [perceives] the water-element... [and so on].
the fire-body … the air-body … the hair-body …
the body of hair … the body of skin … the body of hide …
the body of flesh … the body of blood … the body of sinews …
One contemplates the body of bones … the body of bone-marrow as impermanent, not as permanent;
one contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasure.
He contemplates it as non-self, not as self;
he becomes disenchanted with it, not delighted by it;
he becomes dispassionate toward it, not attached to it; he causes its cessation, not its origination.
He relinquishes and does not grasp.
Contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure;
contemplating as non-self, he abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight; becoming dispassionate...
He abandons lust; by ceasing [craving], he abandons its origination; by relinquishing, he abandons grasping.
In these seven ways he contemplates the body.
The body is the foundation, not the mindfulness itself.
Mindfulness is both the establishment [of mindfulness] and mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that body.
Therefore, it is said:
“Mindfulness-establishment as contemplation of the body in the body.

As for development: there are four kinds of development—development in the sense of non-excess of the states arisen therein; development in the sense of single function (taste) of the faculties; development in the sense of the driving of energy directed toward that; and development in the sense of repetition.
Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body.
How does he dwell contemplating feelings in feelings?
Here, someone contemplates a pleasant feeling as impermanent, not as permanent... [and so on].
He relinquishes; he does not grasp.
Contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence … pe … relinquishing, he abandons grasping.
One contemplates feeling through these seven aspects.
Feeling is the foundation, but not the mindfulness;
mindfulness is both the foundation and the mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that feeling.
Therefore, it is called "the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings in feelings."
“Development” means the four kinds of development … [as above] … development in the sense of repeated practice … here someone [experiences] a painful feeling … [as above].
a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling … a sensual pleasant feeling … a spiritual pleasant feeling …
a worldly painful feeling … an unworldly painful feeling … a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling …
... non-sensual feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant ...
feeling born of eye-contact ... feeling born of ear-contact ... [feeling born of nose-contact ... feeling born of tongue-contact ... feeling born of body-contact ... feeling born of mind-contact ...
feeling born of nose-contact … feeling born of tongue-contact … feeling born of body-contact …
He contemplates feeling born of mind-contact as impermanent, not as permanent; ... [and so on] ...
he relinquishes it, he does not grasp at it.
Contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence; ... [and so on] ...
Relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
In these seven ways, one contemplates feeling.
Feeling is the establishment (upaṭṭhāna), not the mindfulness itself.
Mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that feeling.
Therefore it is said:
“Mindfulness-establishment of contemplation of feelings in feelings.
As for development: there are four kinds of development...
[as before] ...in this way he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings.
How does one dwell contemplating the mind as mind?
Here, someone contemplates a lustful mind as impermanent, not as permanent... [and so on] ...
he relinquishes it, he does not grasp at it.
Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence … [and so on] … relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
In these seven ways, one contemplates the mind.
The mind is the establishment, but not the mindfulness.
Mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that mind.
Therefore it is said:
“The foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the mind as mind.
As for “development,” there are four kinds of development … [and so on].
Development in the sense of repeated practice:
here someone [develops] a mind free from lust … pe … a mind accompanied by hatred … [and so on].
A mind free from hatred...
a deluded mind...
a mind free from delusion...
A contracted mind...
a distracted mind...
an exalted mind...
The non-exalted mind...
the surpassable mind...
the unsurpassable mind...
A concentrated mind … an unconcentrated mind … a liberated mind …
The unliberated mind … eye-consciousness … ear-consciousness …
nose-consciousness … tongue-consciousness … body-consciousness …
He contemplates mind-consciousness as impermanent, not as permanent … [and so on] … he relinquishes it, he does not grasp it.
Contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence … [and so on] …
Relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
One contemplates the mind through these seven aspects.
The mind is the establishment (upaṭṭhāna), not the mindfulness (sati).
Mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness itself.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that mind.
Therefore it is said:
“Mindfulness-establishment as the contemplation of mind in the mind.
Development means the fourfold development … [and so on] … development in the sense of repeated practice.
Thus he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind.
How does he dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena?
Here, someone—setting aside the body, setting aside feeling, and setting aside the mind—contemplates the remaining phenomena as impermanent, not as permanent.
He contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasure;
he contemplates it as non-self, not as self;
he becomes disenchanted with it, not delighted by it.
He becomes dispassionate, not passionate;
he causes cessation, not origination;
he relinquishes, he does not grasp.
Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure;
contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust;
causing cessation, one abandons origination; relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
One contemplates those phenomena through these seven aspects.
Phenomena are the foundation, but not mindfulness;
mindfulness is both the foundation and mindfulness itself.
With that mindfulness and with that knowledge, one contemplates those phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena in phenomena."
"Bhāvanā" means the four kinds of development:

there is development in the sense of non-transgression of the states arisen therein; development in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties; development in the sense of the driving of the energy directed toward that; and development in the sense of repeated practice.
Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.
The Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished.
